newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Gold and dollar fall, Euro bourses mixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gold and dollar fall, Euro bourses mixed.

text.p: Gold slid $9 an ounce to new 12-year lows around $315 on Monday morning, making a total drop of around $50 since January and raising concern about the future of some mines.
"It would take a Martian to be bullish at this point," said Andy Smith, precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland.
"Expect an orgy of selling over the next few weeks," a bullion dealer added.
On currency markets, the dollar opened the week lower as news of a rising Japanese trade surplus boosted the yen and fresh jitters on European economic and monetary union aided the mark.
The Frankfurt bourse hit a record high, but fears of higher interest rates spooked the London stock market and Paris showed little net change.
London strategists expected Wall Street to continue its record-breaking run as investors returned later following the long Independence Day holiday.
Gold plunged to 12-year lows last week after the Reserve Bank of Australia said it had sold 167 tonnes from its gold reserves.

Following disposals earlier in the 1990s by the Belgian and Dutch central banks, this pushed already nervous investors to sell for fear more central banks would offload some of the 35,000 tonnes of gold they own.
The yen was boosted to four-week highs near 112 to the dollar in earlier Asian trading after news of a 129.3-percent year-on-year gain in Japan's trade surplus for the first 20 days of June.
"Things have calmed down since this morning, but people are reluctant to be short yen as long as the trade issue is still alive," said a Japanese bank dealer.
The dollar also came under pressure as the pound lost around two pfennigs due to data showing a sharp drop in British industrial output, which analysts attributed mainly to sterling's strength.
The U.S. currency suffered further from market nerves over Europe's unsteady progress towards economic and monetary union (EMU).
As some senior German politicians continue to speak out for a delay in EMU, rather than softening qualification criteria, the mark has gained favour.

In an interview in the Financial Times, Bavarian prime minister Edmund Stoiber, a member of the Christian Social Union party of Theo Waigel, Germany's finance minister, said an EMU delay would be preferable to a weak single currency.
"A controlled delay would certainly be better than a weak European currency," Stoiber was quoted as saying. "It would mean holding to the goal of the euro and holding firm to the criteria."

The London stock market was dragged down from early gains by a fall in futures and bonds amid speculation of an interest rate rise this week by the newly-independent Bank of England to keep the economy from overheating.
"The futures dragged us back this morning. People are just waiting for the rate rise at the monetary policy meeting (on Thursday)," said one senior dealer.

Britain's latest building society-turned-bank to float on the stock market, Woolwich, provided a rare bright point. It topped its tipped debut level of around 320 pence at 343 but was well below an earlier high of 370.

The Paris bourse erased early losses, prompted by the lower dollar and technical reasons, to show little net change, while Frankfurt kept up its record-breaking act with a gain of around three-quarters of a percentage point.
CURRENCIES AT 1130 GMT
The dollar was around 112.25 yen and 1.7452 marks, compared with 113.74 and 1.7565 in late European business on Friday.
Sterling was around 2.9390 marks versus 2.9597 late on Friday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1130 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 31.4 points or 0.65 percent at 4,781.4.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 29.43 points or 0.75 percent at 3,971.96 after an earlier record 3,974.79.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was 3.76 points or 0.13 percent higher at 2,938.24.
PRECIOUS METALS
London gold was fixed in the morning at $318.75 an ounce, well down from Friday's late London level of $324.50, and then dropped further to around $315.50. Silver declined seven cents to $4.48.
